text: [excited] This is Max. Max just read his entire chemistry textbook. Once. In the bathroom. And now he knows every word. Every diagram. The coffee stain on page two hundred and twelve. Exam? Four minutes. One hundred percent. [deadpan] The teacher had to sit down. Because this morning, Max's memory got one hundred times better. Which sounds amazing. And for about a week... it is. [pause] Then it ruins his life. Slowly. In alphabetical order. [tense] By day thirty, Max will beg to forget. And one memory... nearly gets him killed.

[curious] So how good is "a hundred times better"? Here's you. You learn something today... and by tomorrow, about two thirds of it is gone. That's not you being lazy. That's normal. It's called the forgetting curve, and everyone's on it. Max? Max isn't on the curve. Max is a straight line. Forever. The world's top memory athletes can learn a shuffled deck of cards in about fifteen seconds. Max does it before you've finished shuffling. And your brain can hold a lot. By one estimate, around two and a half petabytes. That's roughly three million hours of TV. Max intends to use all of it.

[excited] Day one. Max learns French. Day two. Spanish. Day three. Japanese, Arabic and, for some reason, Klingon. He never loses his keys. [sarcastic] Unlike some of us. He wins every argument, because he remembers exactly what you said. Word for word. With the date. Quiz night? Banned. For life. Passwords? He has three hundred, all different, none written down. Birthdays? He remembers everyone's. Including Dave's dog. Sir Biscuit. Born the fourth of March. Allergic to cheese. [warm] For one week, Max is the most useful person alive. [pause] And then. He goes to bed. [whisper] And the real problem hasn't even started yet.

[quiet] Here's something nobody tells you. At night, your brain doesn't just rest. It cleans up. It sorts the day, keeps what matters... and quietly bins the rest. What you had for lunch three Tuesdays ago? Binned. What that stranger was wearing on the bus? Binned. Max's brain doesn't have a bin. So everything stays. Every face, every sound, every second. Including... the Wave. [slow] March 2014. A woman waved. Max waved back. She was waving at the guy behind him. You've forgotten your version of this. Max can't. He relives it in full HD. Surround sound. Every night. [deadpan] It now has a director's cut.

[curious] And this isn't made up. There was a real man like Max. Russia, the 1920s. A journalist named Solomon Shereshevsky. His boss noticed he never took notes. So scientists tested him. Long lists of numbers, words, nonsense. He remembered them all. Then he remembered them again... fifteen years later. Sounds like a superpower. But here's what the scientist studying him noticed. Solomon struggled to recognise faces. Because a face is never the same twice. Smiling, frowning, different light. He remembered every version... so none of them matched. [pause] Max's mum is not thrilled. And that's the big secret. Forgetting isn't your brain failing. Forgetting is your brain working. When you forget the details, you keep the pattern. You don't remember every dog you've ever met. You just know... "dog". Max remembers every dog. Individually. So when he sees a new one... his brain just goes "error". [pause] Except Sir Biscuit. He'd know Sir Biscuit anywhere. [tense] Funny, right? It stops being funny on a Tuesday. At a crossing.

[tense] Week three. Max's head is full of everything, all the time. Someone says "sandwich", and his brain plays every sandwich he's ever eaten. In order. With the receipts. He can't read a joke, because a joke needs you to forget the obvious meaning first. [sarcastic] Comedy is dead to him. Which is a shame, because this video is hilarious. He can't make simple choices. Pick a restaurant? He remembers every meal he's had at every one of them. [tense] Then comes that Tuesday. Max steps off the kerb, and the green man reminds him of a green jumper. Which reminds him of a birthday. Which reminds him of a cake. Which reminds him of every cake. Ever. [urgent] He's not looking at the road any more. He's looking at two thousand and nine. [shouting] Max! [pause] Real life comes back at the very last second. [shaky] Your brain filters out the past so you can see the present. Max's can't. [quiet] And the worst part: bad memories don't fade. For you, an embarrassing day turns into a funny story. Time sands the edges off. For Max, the edges never come off. Every argument, every goodbye, every awkward silence stays sharp. [heavy] One woman who lives with a real version of this, called hyperthymesia, described it as "nonstop, uncontrollable, and totally exhausting". Scientists have only confirmed a few dozen people like her. Most of us will never meet one. [building] And then comes the night it all happens at once. Every memory he's ever had. All playing. At the same time. [whisper] Including the Wave.

[gentle] So what does Max actually want? Not a better memory. A worse one. Just a little. Because here's what you've got, right now, for free: a brain that keeps what matters... and lets the rest slip away. That's how you get over things. That's how you learn rules instead of lists. That's how a bad day becomes a funny story. Forgetting isn't a bug. [pause] It's the best feature you've got.

[warm] As for Max? He turned it down to about twice as good as you. He still remembers birthdays. He still never loses his keys. And he has finally, finally forgotten the Wave. [pause] ...Oh no. [laughing] Some things you never learn.
What's the one thing you wish you could forget? Tell us in the comments. Or don't. We'll forget it anyway. Wait... where did I put my keys?
